name: API abuse / bot defence / WAF feature backend (edge / platform)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: API abuse / bot defence / WAF feature backend at the edge or API-gateway layer
domain_fit.one_line_definition: An edge proxy, API gateway or WAAP decides in <10 ms on every API request whether to allow, throttle, challenge or block based on adaptive per-(IP, API-key, route, status_class) rolling rates, behavioral burst signals and low-and-slow pattern features computed from the live request stream.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Power adaptive per-(IP, API-key, route) rate limiting that is tighter than a static token bucket — e.g. tighten the budget automatically when a key's 1m rolling 4xx/5xx ratio jumps. 2) Detect 'low-and-slow' abuse where a single client stays under any single rate limit but the cross product (key x route x status_class) is anomalous over 1h–24h. 3) Detect behavioral bursts on previously-quiet keys / IPs (the 'parked key suddenly hits /signup 500 times' signal). 4) Feed bot-management / WAAP scorers (Cloudflare BM, Datadome, HUMAN, Kasada, Castle, Imperva, Wallarm) with consistent per-entity velocity/rate features across edge PoPs. 5) Drive OWASP API4:2023 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption) and API6:2023 (Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows) controls with real features instead of static thresholds.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Wire events are HTTP request records emitted by the proxy on every API call: request {ts, ip, ip_asn, api_key_hash, route_template, http_method, status, latency_ms, bytes_in, bytes_out, ja3/ja4, user_agent_hash, country, tls_version, content_type, auth_type}. Optional supporting events: auth_failure {ts, ip, api_key_hash, reason}, captcha_challenge {ts, ip, outcome}, waf_rule_hit {ts, ip, rule_id, severity}. Volume is dominated by the request event; everything else is sampled or per-decision.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of counters, rates, n_unique and distributions over 1s / 10s / 1m / 5m / 1h / 24h sliding windows. Per-(api_key, route): rate(requests), rate(4xx), rate(5xx), failure_ratio = (4xx+5xx)/total, n_unique(ip), distribution(status_class). Per-(ip, route): velocity, n_unique(api_key) (key-rotation / spraying), n_unique(route) (catalog traversal / enumeration). Per-(api_key) global: rate(requests), distribution(route) (route-mix shift = abuse), distance(usual_geo, current_geo), entropy(inter_request_gap_ms) (low std-dev catches low-and-slow bots that pace themselves). Per-route global: rate(requests), rate(5xx) (back-pressure to adaptively tighten limits when upstream degrades). Per-(asn, route): rate(requests), failure_ratio (cross-IP ASN-level spray detection).
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite. Primary keys are IP (v4/v6), API-key-hash, JWT-subject-hash, route_template, ASN, ja3/ja4 fingerprint, and the cross products (ip x route), (api_key x route), (api_key x status_class), (asn x route), (ja4 x route). Route_template (not raw path) is the discriminating grain — /users/{id} not /users/12345 — and the API gateway is responsible for emitting it.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate (1s, 10s, 1m, 5m, 1h, 24h). Approximate aggregates (HLL for n_unique-IP-per-key, CMS / Top-K for top routes per key) are acceptable on the explosive IP / fingerprint axes. Tumbling windows are useful for billing/quota accounting (where double-counting is unacceptable). Session windows are useful for 'burst then quiet' bot patterns but not strictly required if 10s and 1m sliding counters exist. Sub-second windows (1s, 10s) matter at this layer in a way they did not for #2 — at the gateway the decision is inline on every request, and a 1s rate sees a credential-spray ramp earlier than a 1m rate.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once is acceptable for risk scoring and adaptive rate features (double-counting biases the velocity feature upward, which is the safe direction for abuse detection). Strict exactly-once is required only if beava is also driving paid-quota / billing accounting on the same counters — most buyers run a separate, exact quota counter for that, and use beava-style features only for the abuse signal.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Read p99 <5 ms is the operational target; <10 ms is the hard ceiling because every request decision is inline at the proxy. Datadome publicly reports <2 ms per request at the edge, which is the bar competitors are measured against. beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get fits well inside this budget if co-located on the same host/PoP; an off-host hop would already eat half the budget.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to single-digit seconds end-to-end. A credential-stuffing or API-key-rotation wave can ramp from 0 to tens of thousands of requests per second in seconds (Cloudflare and Akamai both report multi-billion-request/day attack waves); features that lag by even 10 seconds defeat 1s-window detectors. beava's push-on-event model with no broker hop fits this — but only if the proxy can push events synchronously or near-synchronously alongside the decision read.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state is extremely write-heavy: every request is one write and one batch_get. Mid-size API platforms run 100M–10B requests/day (~1k–100k EPS average); edge buyers (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, Cloudfront) proxy hundreds of billions/day across their networks. A single beava node at the published ~684k EPS (M4, TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) covers a regional shard of a mid-size API gateway or a single tenant of a WAAP vendor; a global edge buyer needs horizontal partitioning that beava v0 does not provide in-process. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Roughly 1:1 — every request produces one write (the event) and one batch_get (the decision). Slightly read-skewed at gateways that aggregate multiple feature reads (~20–50 features) per decision. Distinctly less read-heavy than recsys / personalization, distinctly less write-heavy than ad-tech telemetry.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by IP cardinality. A mid-size API platform sees ~1–10M distinct IPs/day and ~10k–100k active API keys; route_template cardinality is bounded (low thousands). At ~200 B per per-entity feature vector, that is single-digit GB for keys/routes (fits trivially) and 1–20 GB for IPs (fits on one box with TTL). An edge buyer at hundreds of millions of distinct IPs/day would need sharding and aggressive TTL/eviction to stay in RAM. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Bounded on route_template (low thousands per tenant), slowly-growing on api_key (thousands to millions across a SaaS platform's customers), explosive on IP (especially behind residential-proxy networks rotating millions of /32s), explosive on (ip x route), bounded on JA4 (low thousands of distinct fingerprints globally), bounded on ASN (~70k allocated). The (ip x route) cross-product is the dangerous one — naively materialized it is unbounded; HLL / CMS approximate primitives are the fix.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Sub-seconds to minutes for hot velocity features (1s/10s/1m/5m sliding windows). 1h–24h for medium-term per-key / per-route reputation. 7–30 d for long-term API-key abuse reputation feeding ML scorers; beyond that, the buyer is typically exporting to a SIEM / lakehouse. Aggressive per-key TTL is essential because IP cardinality blows up under DDoS-class events.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20–80 features per inline request decision is typical for a WAAP / bot-management buyer (per-IP rate, per-IP failure-ratio, per-key rate, per-key route-mix entropy, per-(key x route) rate, per-ASN spray, per-JA4 cluster, plus a handful of static-rule lookups). Strongly favors a batch_get path — exactly what beava ships.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe. The features are derived risk signals, not money. If a node loses its 1m sliding window during a restart, the buyer's adaptive limits degrade for a few minutes but no regulatory or financial obligation is broken. beava's WAL + snapshot is more than enough; many edge buyers would prefer beava with WAL disabled in exchange for higher throughput. The hard problem is cold-start replay time after a crash with multi-GB hot state.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Excellent fit for edge / sidecar / PoP topologies. Buyers in this space are explicitly pushing detection logic to the edge (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, AWS WAF rate-based rules, Akamai EdgeWorkers, Kong / Tyk gateway plugins) because origin round-trips are too slow for inline decisions. beava's single-binary, no-broker, push-on-event model maps directly to a per-PoP or per-cluster sidecar. The hard limits are: (a) beava v0 has no in-process sharding so a single tenant beyond ~684k EPS or ~50 GB hot state must be hand-sharded externally; (b) global edge buyers want cross-PoP feature replication / merging which beava does not ship; (c) beava refuses on network-FS, so the WAL must live on local disk in each PoP.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Platform / infrastructure / SecOps / edge-engineering teams at: (a) CDN / edge / WAAP vendors (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, CloudFront, F5, Imperva), (b) standalone bot-management / API-protection vendors (Datadome, HUMAN, Kasada, Arkose, Castle, Fingerprint, Cequence, Wallarm, Salt Security, Noname / Akamai, 42Crunch), (c) API-gateway / API-management vendors (Kong, Apigee / Google, Tyk, KrakenD, Zuplo, Mulesoft), (d) identity / fraud-prevention vendors that have an edge surface (Stytch, Curity, Auth0/Okta), and (e) large in-house platform / SRE / SecOps teams at SaaS, fintech, gaming, e-commerce. Distinctly NOT the corporate fraud team (that's #2 / #1a-c) — buyer here is platform-eng / edge-eng / SecOps.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Bot management is a $1.0–1.3B market in 2025–2026, projected to $2.1–4.9B by 2030 at 19–24% CAGR (multiple analyst estimates). The broader API security market is $1.8B in 2026 projected to $5.7B by 2030 at ~33% CAGR (SNS Insider). Major M&A signal: Akamai acquired Noname Security for $450M in June 2024, signalling enterprise demand. Vendor pricing scale: Datadome runs $1,990–$4,000/mo for 10–30M requests; Kasada $2,500–$4,000/mo for 10–20M requests; Castle starts ~$200/mo for 100k requests; Wallarm/Salt/Noname/42Crunch enterprise contracts are six- to seven-figure ACVs. Edge buyer scale: Cloudflare ML trains on hundreds of billions of requests/day. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 elevated 'Unrestricted Resource Consumption' (API4) and 'Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows' (API6), explicitly framing the problem as needing rate / behavioral controls beyond a static token bucket. 2) Credential-stuffing attacks targeting APIs reportedly up ~45% YoY in 2026 (Wallarm 2026 API ThreatStats); only 21% of orgs report strong API attack detection. 3) Residential-proxy abuse and AI-generated traffic make IP-only rate limiting ineffective — buyers must combine per-IP, per-key, per-ASN, per-JA4 features in real time. 4) Agentic-AI traffic surge (Anthropic Computer Use, OpenAI Operator, ChatGPT browsing) is producing high-volume legitimate-but-bot-shaped traffic that static WAFs misclassify; vendors are racing to ship adaptive per-route features (Cloudflare 'per-customer defenses' Nov 2025, Arkose Titan Jan 2026, Stytch Intelligent Rate Limiting 2025). 5) Akamai's June 2024 $450M Noname acquisition and Cloudflare's continuous bot-management investment are pulling enterprise budget into the category. 6) Multi-region regulators (DORA in EU, Jan 2025; PSD3 / PSR ~mid-2026 for payments) tighten operational-resilience requirements on API rate-limit and abuse controls for financial APIs.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: OWASP API Top 10 2023 (API4, API6, API8 — security misconfiguration including rate-limit) is the de-facto compliance frame and most buyers reference it explicitly. DORA (in force Jan 17, 2025) imposes ICT operational-resilience obligations including third-party / API exposure controls for EU financial firms. PSD3 / PSR1 (~mid-2026) covers PSP APIs and broadens SCA-style monitoring to login / mandate / beneficiary endpoints. GDPR / CCPA (IP and API-key hashes are personal data — argues for short TTLs and salted hashes). PCI-DSS for payment-API gateways. SOC 2 for any vendor — most buyers will require auditable retention, access control, and TLS-in-transit, which beava v0 does not ship. ISO 27001 indirectly. NIST SP 800-53 SI-4 / AC-7 for federal API gateways.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast — 1–3 days to a working demo of per-(api_key, route, status_class) rolling rates with the @bv.event + @bv.table primitives, plus a thin Envoy / Nginx / Kong / Tyk Lua-or-Wasm shim that pushes the request event and pulls the batch_get. 2–6 weeks to a production pilot at an API-gateway vendor once auth and TLS are added (the v0 gaps below) and once the integration with an existing rules engine (OPA, Coraza, Tyk middleware, Apigee policies) is wired. Demo videos selling the 'per-(key, route, status_class) anomaly' story should be straightforward.

competition.incumbents: Generic real-time stack: Redis (counters + Lua, Redis Stack with Bloom / CMS / Top-K) is the overwhelming default for hand-rolled rate limiters; Memcached and DragonflyDB for simpler counters. Cloudflare Durable Objects for serverless-edge rate counters (soft-limit ~1k req/s per DO, sharding required above). AWS WAF rate-based rules and Cloudflare WAF rate-limiting rules (managed). Open-source: Coraza WAF + OWASP CRS (proxy-wasm filter) for the rule layer with no native feature store; Envoy local + global rate-limit service (Lyft ratelimit) for the counter layer. Flink / Materialize / RisingWave for buyers who already have Kafka and want SQL-on-streams. Online feature stores (Tecton, Hopsworks, Chalk, Fennel) are an awkward fit at the edge — they target ML serving from a central warehouse, not in-line WAF decisions.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Cloudflare Bot Management (ML + JA4 + multi-engine, hundreds of billions of req/day training data), Akamai Bot Manager + Noname API Security ($450M acquisition June 2024), Datadome (sub-2ms edge integrations, CDN-agnostic), HUMAN (formerly PerimeterX), Kasada, Arkose Labs (Titan platform Jan 2026 with 24/7 SOC), Castle (behavioral integrity with Cloudflare integration May 2025), Fingerprint (Velocity Signals product — 5m/1h/24h counters per visitorID/linkedID/IP, very close to beava's primitive shape), Imperva (Thales), F5 / Shape (Distributed Cloud Bot Defense), Netacea, Cequence, Wallarm, Salt Security, 42Crunch, IPQS, Fraudlogix. API-gateway-side: Kong (Konnect, with rate-limiting-advanced plugin using Redis), Apigee (Google), Tyk (Redis sliding window log limiter with DRL), Zuplo (globally synchronized edge rate limiting), KrakenD, Mulesoft, AWS API Gateway.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Redis cluster — fits the per-PoP / per-cluster sidecar topology this market has standardized on. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives (counters, n_unique, velocity, rate, distribution, distance, entropy) cover the per-(IP, key, route, status_class) features this domain literally lives on, without writing Lua / Wasm / Flink SQL. 3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get is inside the <5ms inline-decision budget that the WAAP market is measured on (Datadome publishes <2ms, Cloudflare DO ~1k req/s per shard). 4) Apache-2.0 with no open-core — attractive to gateway vendors (Kong / Tyk / Apigee / Zuplo) and bot-management vendors (Castle / Fingerprint / Datadome) that want to embed it rather than depend on a competitor's managed cloud or a Redis-Source-Available license. 5) Push-on-event model maps directly to how proxies already emit access logs (Envoy access-log filter, Nginx access_log, Coraza audit log) — no broker hop. 6) The composite-key story ((ip x route), (key x status_class), (asn x route)) is first-class via @bv.table, not bolted on as a Redis key-naming convention. 7) Fingerprint's 'Velocity Signals' product (per VisitorID/LinkedID/IP at 5m/1h/24h) is essentially the productized form of one slice of what beava ships as a generic primitive set — strong validation of the shape.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 in v0 — disqualifying for any production deployment by a regulated buyer or any vendor that needs mTLS between the proxy and the feature backend. 2) No in-process sharding — a single tenant beyond ~684k EPS or ~50 GB hot state must be hand-sharded externally; an edge buyer doing global bot management is far beyond one box. 3) No cross-node / cross-PoP feature replication or merge — global rate limiting (Zuplo's pitch) is not possible without external coordination, and Cloudflare's Durable Objects model is purpose-built to solve exactly this. 4) Refuse-on-network-FS + in-memory only means each PoP must plan local-disk WAL and bounded cold-start replay time; an IP-cardinality blowup during a DDoS-class event could OOM the node. 5) No triggers / 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — adaptive rate limiting really wants 'tighten this key's budget when 1m failure_ratio > 0.4', and today that has to be polled. 6) No multi-tenancy primitives — a WAAP vendor serving many customers needs per-tenant namespaces, quotas and isolation that beava doesn't ship. 7) No first-class HLL / CMS / Top-K in the documented primitive set (it may exist in the 50+ primitives — needs to be documented prominently for the (ip x route) cross-product). [uncertain] 8) No secondary indexes / no 'list top-k IPs by failure_ratio in last 5 min' — limits the SOC / analyst surface. 9) Python SDK is great for the ML / data-team author; gateway buyers (Cloudflare, Kong, Tyk, Envoy) live in Rust / Go / C++ / Lua / Wasm — beava's TCP+msgpack wire is languageagnostic, but a Rust / Go / Lua / Wasm client SDK story needs to exist for this market.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: edge proxies and API gateways emitting per-request events — Cloudflare Workers (Rate Limiting API + Durable Objects), Fastly Compute, Envoy (access-log filter, ext_proc, Lua filter, Wasm filter), Nginx (njs, Lua), Caddy, Kong (plugins in Lua / Go), Tyk (Go / JS middleware), Apigee (JavaScript / Java callouts), AWS API Gateway (Lambda authorizer / WAF rate-based rules), Coraza WAF (proxy-wasm), OPA/Envoy plugin. beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 fits the Worker / serverless producer; TCP+msgpack :8081 fits the high-throughput Envoy / Nginx / Kong path. Consumers: rules engines (Coraza CRS, ModSecurity, OPA policies, Tyk middleware, Apigee policies, Cloudflare Workers logic, custom Lua/Wasm) and ML scorers (XGBoost / LightGBM / ONNX served from a separate process pulling features via batch_get) and direct in-proxy allow/deny/challenge logic.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. The dominant pattern is a deterministic rules layer (per-(IP, route) rate > X, per-key failure-ratio > Y) combined with an ML risk scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / deep model) consuming the same features. beava as a pure feature backend stays decoupled from the scorer — natural seam. Concretely: Cloudflare BM is an ML scorer with a rules layer on top; Coraza / OWASP CRS is pure rules; Castle / Fingerprint / Datadome / HUMAN are scorer-plus-rules products. beava feeds all of them identically.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public users of beava on this use case yet. [uncertain] Comparable production systems and their public docs: Cloudflare Bot Management (per-customer behavioral baselines blog, Nov 2025), Cloudflare Workers Rate Limiting API and Durable Objects rate-limit docs, Fingerprint Velocity Signals (the closest commercial analog to beava's primitive shape — per-visitor/linkedID/IP at 5m/1h/24h), Datadome ($1,990–$4k/mo enterprise tier, sub-2ms inline), Stytch Intelligent Rate Limiting (device-level, 2025), Castle's edge integrations with Cloudflare (May 2025), Auth0's JA4-based bot detection (2025), Akamai/Noname acquisition ($450M, June 2024), Arkose Titan platform (Jan 2026, 24/7 SOC). Wallarm 2026 API ThreatStats report cites ~45% YoY increase in API credential-stuffing attacks.

[uncertain] Broader community is very active: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (API4 / API6 cheat sheets), Cloudflare blog on per-customer bot defenses (Nov 2025), Auth0 blog on JA4 signals (2025), Arcjet / Tyk / Zuplo / Kong rate-limiting comparison content, Hacker News threads on Cloudflare DO rate limiters and 'I built my own bot defence' DEV.to writeups, Reddit r/devops r/netsec r/sysadmin threads on residential-proxy waves and OWASP API Top 10. adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No dedicated API-abuse / WAF-feature-backend demo identified in the repository as of the snapshot reviewed. The repository has fraud, adtech and ecommerce demos under /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/ but no api_abuse or waf_features example. The closest analog is the bot-defence shape captured in the existing fraud demo, but the route / api_key / status_class entity grain is distinct enough to warrant its own example. [uncertain]
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Maximum. This is one of the most actively adversarial domains in the stack — attackers retool weekly (residential-proxy rotation, JA4-spoofing toolkits, headless-browser polymorphism, AI-driven request generators, agentic-AI traffic that is bot-shaped but legitimate). Feature drift is rapid; the buyer expects to add and retire features continuously, which argues for a developer-ergonomic feature backend (beava's @bv.event / @bv.table model) over a SQL-on-Flink pipeline or a Redis-Lua snowflake.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Long historical lookback / batch backfill — beava is in-memory only, not the place to store a 30-day API access log for retrospective analysis (that belongs in Parquet / a lakehouse / a SIEM). 2) Acting as the WAF itself — beava sits behind one (Coraza / ModSecurity / Cloudflare WAF / AWS WAF), feeding it features. 3) Acting as the rules engine or the ML scorer — beava is the feature backend, not the policy decision point. 4) Cross-entity joins ('show me all API keys that share an IP with this ASN cluster') — beava has no join engine; that's a graph-DB / OLAP / SIEM problem. 5) Full audit-grade request archive / forensic replay — WAL is for crash recovery, not for compliance retention. 6) Strict exactly-once paid-quota / billing counters where double-counting is unacceptable — buyers should keep a separate exact counter (Stripe-style idempotency-key dedupe) for billing; beava covers the abuse signal. 7) Global single-source-of-truth rate-limit coordination across PoPs (Zuplo / Cloudflare-DO pitch) — beava v0 is not designed for cross-region feature merge. 8) Replacing the regulatory-grade event store for AML-style retention (different domain, different SLO profile).
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination and mutual TLS on :8081 / :8090, plus an auth model (token, mTLS, or both) on the admin / push surfaces — without this, no edge-vendor or WAAP buyer can deploy it externally. This is the single biggest blocker. 2) Triggers / 'callback when counter crosses threshold' — adaptive WAF is inherently event-driven (tighten the budget when failure_ratio > X), and polling 20–80 features per inline request to threshold them adds avoidable round-trips on the hot path. 3) In-process or sidecar sharding by key prefix, so a single tenant beyond ~684k EPS scales within one cluster without external hand-sharding. 4) HLL / Bloom / CMS / Top-K approximate primitives as first-class, prominently-documented aggregations to bound (ip x route) cross-product memory under DDoS-class events. 5) Per-key TTL / sliding-window eviction so explosive IP cardinality doesn't OOM the box during attack spikes. 6) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, quotas, and per-tenant rate-limit accounting for WAAP vendors serving many customers. 7) Rust / Go / C++ client SDKs (and ideally Lua / Wasm) — the buyer ecosystem here lives in proxies, not Python services. The wire is already language-agnostic; the SDK matrix is the gap. 8) Cross-PoP feature merge / replication story (CRDT-style counters, gossip, or anti-entropy) for buyers who want one logical view of (api_key) state across regions — Cloudflare Durable Objects is the bar to clear here. 9) A streaming admin / debug surface ('top-k IPs by failure_ratio in last 5 min') so SOC analysts can drive incident response without materializing the full keyspace. 10) Hooks for residential-proxy / ASN / JA3-JA4 enrichment (in-process modules or a documented producer pattern). 11) Bounded cold-start WAL replay benchmarks with multi-GB hot state; a node restart during an active attack must not become an outage. 12) GDPR / CCPA-friendly defaults — salted IP hashing at rest, short default TTLs, documented PII model.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — this domain genuinely needs an event-driven trigger primitive (e.g. 'when (api_key x route).failure_ratio crosses 0.4 in last 10s, fire a webhook to the gateway to tighten the budget / challenge / quarantine'), not just feature serving. Inline-decision reads cover the synchronous path, but the asynchronous 'spawn CAPTCHA / send to SOC / lower the per-key budget / push a Coraza rule update' path is wasteful when implemented as repeated batch_get polling. This is one of the most-cited gaps for the domain.
